absent: Live per-task summation and sample storage layout behind group CPU totals.
Arming, expiry delivery and notification behavior for virtual and profiling CPU timers.
Remaining-time query and old-value translation details for wall-clock high-resolution timer.
Numeric values of tick rate, user tick rate and per-second time constants.
Proc sysctl table wiring, permissions and range data for tick tunables.
Write path that sets time namespace monotonic and boot-time offsets.
Virtual data mapping lifecycle and fault behavior beyond invalidation walk.
Signal or callback actions performed when an interval timer expires.

findings.text: Group CPU accounting keeps per-category totals that never move backward. An update comparing a freshly summed value with the stored atomic counter leaves the stored value unchanged when the candidate is not larger and otherwise retries a compare exchange until it installs the larger value. The combined updater applies this forward-only rule to user time, system time and total execution time together.

Sampling of thread-group CPU clocks follows an active flag. When the flag shows inactive, a plain sampler sums live per-task values directly, while a starting sampler first synchronizes atomic storage from live totals and then marks the flag active before sampling from atomic storage. Once the flag shows active, sampling reads the atomic snapshot path.

Starting group CPU accounting expects the caller to already hold the target sighand protection. The active flag itself is checked and later stored with single-copy access without holding an extra lock, relying on the forward-only atomic updater to tolerate concurrent publishers.

Interval timer value validation accepts only specifications whose seconds field is not negative and whose microseconds field lies strictly below one second worth of microseconds. Both the initial expiry and the repeat interval must satisfy this rule.

One central setter implements all interval timers. A wall-clock selector uses a high-resolution timer owned by shared signal state, while virtual and profiling selectors delegate to CPU-consumption handling. Any other selector is rejected as invalid.

The wall-clock interval path holds the signal spin lock with interrupts disabled while capturing remaining time and period for the old value and while cancelling, rearming or disarming the timer. If cancellation reports that the expiry handler is running, the path releases the lock, waits for the handler to finish and retries. A zero expiry disarms and clears the stored period, while a nonzero expiry stores the new period and arms a relative timeout.
A cleanup helper disarms every interval timer by applying an empty specification to each selector in turn, requesting no old value.

The alarm helper implements a one-shot wall-clock timer with second resolution and no repeat. On narrow word sizes large second counts are clamped. It delegates to the central setter and reports the previous remaining whole seconds, rounding upward when a fractional remainder reaches at least half a second or when only a sub-second remainder remains.

User-facing interval timer entry points accept native and 32-bit compatibility layouts. They copy the user structure, validate both time values, translate seconds plus microseconds into seconds plus nanoseconds, call the central setter, and copy the prior state back when requested. A missing new value is treated as all zero with a one-time warning. Copy faults and validation failures are reported with distinct error codes.

The fallback tick clocksource provides a low-priority time base driven by the tick counter. Its read operation returns the current tick value. It advertises a narrow cycle mask and tick-derived scaling plus a small upper bound on usable cycles.

Reading the full 64-bit tick counter uses a sequence-counter begin and retry loop around the plain tick variable, giving a consistent snapshot without blocking tick updates. The sequence state is cache aligned and paired with the tick lock.

Early initialization can register a refined tick clocksource cloned from the fallback with a slightly higher rating and a distinct name. Its scale factor is recomputed from a supplied cycles-per-second rate using rounded per-tick and nanoseconds-per-tick derivations with extra fixed-point precision.

Tick conversions for control interfaces translate between ticks and seconds, user ticks and milliseconds. Multiplication that would overflow saturates at the unsigned maximum, millisecond-to-tick conversion caps at the maximum usable offset, and tick-to-millisecond conversion rounds upward. Exact small-ratio paths and scaled arithmetic paths are selected by build constants.

Proc control entry points for tick-related tunables handle integer vectors and bounded long vectors. Each delegates through a generic vector conversion dispatcher to direction-specific translators for plain ticks, user ticks, milliseconds, or range-checked milliseconds.
An alternate build of the same conversion dispatchers unconditionally reports unimplemented, so the associated proc controls have no functional path in that configuration.

Translation of namespace-relative expiry times toward host time applies stored offsets only to monotonic and boot-time clock families and returns other clocks unchanged. Inputs below the applicable offset map to zero as already expired, otherwise the offset is subtracted and results beyond the representable maximum are clamped to that maximum.

Creating a time namespace for a new clone reserves a ucount, allocates a zeroed object, allocates virtual data storage, initializes common namespace state, inherits monotonic and boot-time offsets, marks offsets unfrozen and links the object into the namespace tree. Failures unwind reservations and allocations with distinct shortage codes. Copying without the clone flag only takes another reference on the old namespace.

Time namespace release unlinks from the tree, drops ucount and user references, frees common state and virtual storage, then defers final deallocation by a grace period for concurrent traversal. Lookup helpers pin the current or for-children namespace under a task guard. Fork handling adopts the for-children namespace when it differs from the active one and commits task virtual mappings.

Installing a different time namespace is rejected when the caller is multithreaded or lacks administrative capability in both the target user namespace and the caller credential user namespace. On success both the active and for-children references are replaced by the new namespace.

Publication of namespace offsets into virtual clock data happens at most once. The initial namespace and already frozen namespaces return immediately on a fast path. Otherwise a dedicated mutex serializes initialization with a second check under lock before marking offsets frozen and filling clock entries.

Virtual clock initialization converts stored second and nanosecond offsets into per-clock offset records, sets a starting sequence value and selects namespace mode. The monotonic record is replicated across three monotonic flavors and the boot-time record across two boot-time flavors. Auxiliary clocks are initialized as well when the corresponding build option is enabled.

Joining a time namespace after commit walks the task address space under a read guard and invalidates mappings backed by the virtual system data area, forcing later faults to observe the new namespace view.
The fallback tick clocksource advertises the lowest valid rating value one, a 32-bit cycle mask and a maximum usable cycle count of ten.
The interval timer family contains three selectors indexed zero through two, cleared in order by the global cleanup helper.

Two concurrency hazards are handled without extra blocking. Wall-clock reprogramming that races expiry-handler execution drops its lock, waits for completion and retries instead of deadlocking. Concurrent publishers of group CPU totals rely on forward-only compare-exchange retries so no memory barrier is required around activation.

Virtual storage allocation for time namespaces has two build-selected forms, one that always succeeds without allocating and one that allocates a zeroed page and can fail for lack of memory with matching free behavior. Callers propagate allocation failure during namespace cloning.

Direction-specific sysctl translators for tick values pair a user-to-kernel operation with a kernel-to-user operation through generic integer or long conversion helpers, each bound to one of the tick, user-tick or millisecond mapping functions, with range-checked variants selecting bounded dispatch.
A boot-only flag tracks registration state of the fallback tick clocksource.
